Review Finds Single Inertial Sensors and AI Recognize Functional Stroke Activities

A systematic review published in Artificial Intelligence Review has synthesized evidence on artificial intelligence-based human activity recognition for detecting functional activities in individuals recovering from stroke. Researchers searched four major scientific databases—PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus—identifying seventeen studies that met their inclusion criteria, which collectively involved 224 individuals with stroke.

The systematic investigation evaluated current implementations across sensing technologies, target activities, physical settings, and model architectures. According to the authors, artificial intelligence-based human activity recognition represents a promising methodology for detecting functional activity after stroke, offering the potential to support objective and ecologically valid clinical assessment, continuous monitoring, and targeted treatment strategies.

Inertial measurement units served as the predominant sensing modality across the literature, appearing in 12 of the 17 analyzed studies, or 70.6 percent. Notably, multiple reviewed studies demonstrated the technical feasibility of successfully recognizing relevant functional movements and activities using only a single recording device.

Controlled clinical settings hosted the majority of the reviewed research, accounting for 11 of the 17 studies, or 64.7 percent, leaving real-world clinical validation limited to date. Nevertheless, investigators also deployed single-sensor configurations in home-based and simulated-home environments, indicating viable potential for scalable, low-burden, and unobtrusive activity tracking outside formal medical facilities.

In terms of algorithmic modeling, convolutional neural networks were identified as the most frequently implemented deep learning architecture across the included investigations. When traditional machine learning methods were applied, Random Forest emerged as the most common classifier utilized for recognizing functional stroke activities.

The review noted that while multimodal sensing can enrich functional activity characterization, greater hardware and sensor complexity may diminish feasibility for prolonged continuous monitoring at home. Given methodological and reporting limitations such as confounding and reproducibility concerns, the authors concluded that future research must prioritize longitudinal validation in everyday environments, transparent code and data availability, and the enrollment of acute and severely impaired stroke populations.

Subject of Research: Artificial intelligence-based human activity recognition of functional activities after stroke

Article Title: AI-powered human action recognition of functional activities in stroke: a systematic review

Article References: De Masi, E., Deledda, P., D’Arienzo, M., De Lazzari, B., Malfitano, C., Pezzopane, V., Bonnì, S., Koch, G., Negrini, F., Ciancarelli, I., Morone, G., & Martino Cinnera, A. (2026). AI-powered human action recognition of functional activities in stroke: a systematic review. Artificial Intelligence Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10462-026-11753-w

Keywords: human activity recognition, stroke, inertial measurement units, single-sensor monitoring, convolutional neural networks, random forest, functional activities, systematic review, clinical settings, home-based monitoring, multimodal sensing, deep learning, machine learning, remote care, ecological validity, personalized rehabilitation, reproducibility

News Source: Cassandra Pierce. (November 15, 2026). Review Finds Single Inertial Sensors and AI Recognize Functional Stroke Activities. Scienmag.
